transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-06-24
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Haven Security Lead), Carlos Ruiz (Haven Infra), Ella Park (Haven Compliance)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for joining on short notice, um i'm jordan with redwood inference, this is samir our solutions eng, we'll go through audit logs and admin activity capture, then leave time for q's and next steps.
[00:20] Maya Thompson: thanks jordan, appreciate it. quick context: Haven Health is doing an internal SOC2 readiness review; main asks are what we capture in audit logs, export/integration options to our SIEM, retention + legal hold, and who can access admin logs.
[00:35] Samir Patel: perfect, that aligns with what we typically cover. i'll start with what the audit log schema looks like and then go into exports and retention.
[01:05] Samir Patel: so first, captured events: we log admin actions (user creation, role changes, permission grants, policy changes), auth events (login success/fail, sso assertions, token create/revoke), config changes (model pinning, rollout changes, routing policy edits), data access events (export started, export completed, embedding/response access if applicable), and system-level actions (node restarts, infra scaling events). each event has timestamp, actor (user id and email when available), source ip, request id/correlation id, resource type, action, and status.
[02:00] Carlos Ruiz: can you give an example of a log line? like what fields come across when an admin rotates a key or changes a role?
[02:15] Samir Patel: yeah, for admin role change you'd see fields: timestamp, actor.email, actor.id, actor.role, target.user.id, target.user.email, action: role.change, old_role, new_role, request_id, region, service (eg: console or api), and an event_metadata blob with raw payload. we also capture before/after snapshots for config edits when available.
[03:05] Maya Thompson: when you say actor.id/email, is that coming from SSO? we need to map to our corporate directory identity.
[03:15] Samir Patel: yes, if SSO/SAML/OIDC is configured, the logs include federated subject id and the assertion attributes we receive (subject, email, groups). there's a mapping layer so you can see both the redwood-internal user id and the federated identity.
[03:40] Ella Park: is there any PII in the logs? we have to ensure PHI isn't included inadvertently for healthcare compliance.
[03:50] Samir Patel: good question. logs intentionally avoid embedding request payloads that contain user-submitted content; for data access events we log references (e.g., object id) but not the raw prompt or PHI content. we also mask long strings and remove sensitive fields by default. there is a review and redaction pipeline for any exported logs to avoid PHI leakage.
[04:25] Jordan Lee: and encryption at rest — all audit logs stored by Redwood are encrypted using AES-256. customers on Private can bring their own KMS keys via our KMS integration for key rotation policies.
[04:45] Carlos Ruiz: so for KMS if we bring our own key, does Redwood still have any access to plaintext?
[04:55] Samir Patel: with BYOK (bring-your-own-key) the ciphertext keys are managed by your KMS; Redwood can write encrypted blobs but does not have access to the plaintext key material. for hosted deployments we use our managed keys by default but can support customer-managed keys for Private and Dedicated with proper agreements.
[05:20] Maya Thompson: export options — what's supported? we saw mention of S3 and syslog in your docs.
[05:30] Samir Patel: yes, supported exports: push to customer S3 buckets (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS), syslog/CEF to your SIEM collector (over TLS), and webhook streaming for real-time sinks. we also have a managed Kafka connector in Dedicated for high-volume streams. exports can be batched hourly or streamed in near real-time depending on config.
[06:10] Carlos Ruiz: does the S3 export include the full event payload or a curated schema?
[06:20] Samir Patel: the S3 export includes normalized JSON event records by default — there's an export schema (i'll share) and an option to include expanded event_metadata if you opt in. we recommend the normalized schema for SIEM ingestion.
[06:40] Maya Thompson: about retention — what is the default retention window and can we set our own?
[06:50] Samir Patel: default retention on hosted is 90 days for raw logs and 365 days for aggregated/archived events. customers can request extended retention options — for Dedicated/Private you can set retention policies up to multi-year and configure legal hold to prevent deletion. for hosted longer retention is available as an add-on with contractual terms.
[07:30] Ella Park: legal hold — how do you implement a hold if we need to preserve logs for an investigation?
[07:40] Samir Patel: we have a legal hold flag at the account or object level. when applied, retention wipes are suspended and exports for the period are immutable snapshots. we keep an append-only index for held artifacts and provide a retrieval API.
[08:05] Maya Thompson: integration with our SIEM (we use Splunk) — is there an ingestion guide?
[08:15] Samir Patel: yes, we'll provide a Splunk HEC ingestion example, syslog/CEF example, and S3 + Lambda forwarder if you prefer pulling from S3. i'll attach the sample exported logs (redacted) so your SIEM team can validate field mapping.
[08:40] Jordan Lee: just to call out, many enterprise customers forward logs to both a SIEM and an S3 cold store for long-term retention; that's a common pattern.
[08:55] Carlos Ruiz: alerting — do you provide alert hooks for suspicious admin activity?
[09:05] Samir Patel: we have built-in alerting for certain anomalies (multiple failed admin logins, role escalations, large exports). Those can be configured to post to Slack/email or to a webhook for your security tooling. for more advanced detection you can pipe logs into your SIEM and run detection there.
[09:40] Maya Thompson: who can access the logs internally at Redwood? we need to know personnel access and auditability.
[09:50] Samir Patel: access is limited by role-based access control — only designated ops and security roles can view raw logs; access is logged and subject to our internal audit. for Private customers we can agree to a shared access model and limit Redwood support access via just-in-time access and audited access sessions.
[10:20] Ella Park: do you provide an audit trail of who viewed logs?
[10:25] Samir Patel: yes, view/access events are themselves logged as audit events: viewer.id, viewer.role, timestamp, reason (if provided), and session id.
[10:40] Maya Thompson: we have a compliance requirement to keep a tamper-evident chain for admin events. do you provide WORM or hash chaining?
[10:55] Samir Patel: we support append-only indexes and can provide hash chaining for held exports — a signed digest per day that you can verify. For Private deployments you can integrate with your own WORM storage for immutability.
[11:25] Jordan Lee: quick note — some of our product names in docs get auto-corrected, you might see "Redwood Dedicate" shows up in early slides, ignore that — it's Dedicated.
[11:40] Maya Thompson: (laughs) noted. ok a couple more specific Qs: 1) Do you log admin API keys usage? 2) Do export events include destination IPs? 3) Is there session replay or request body logging?
[12:00] Samir Patel: 1) yes, admin API key usage is logged with request id, actor (key id), timestamp, endpoint, and response status. 2) export events include destination host/ip for outbound syslog or S3 endpoint and the bucket/object path. 3) by default we do not log request bodies that contain user content; we capture request metadata and references only. for forensic needs we can enable expanded capture for a narrow scope with consent and additional controls.
[12:50] Carlos Ruiz: what's the size/volume impact? if we enable expanded metadata capture what's the cost?
[13:00] Samir Patel: expanded capture increases log volume — typically 3x-10x depending on payloads. for hosted we charge based on log egress and storage; for Dedicated you size your retention and storage accordingly. we can provide an estimate once we see sample traffic.
[13:35] Maya Thompson: any SLA on log export delivery? we need assurances for timely arrival into our SIEM for monitoring.
[13:45] Samir Patel: for near-real-time streaming, we target sub-2 minute delivery 95% of the time; for batched S3 deliveries it's hourly by default. Dedicated can have tighter SLOs in the contract.
[14:10] Jordan Lee: let's talk about data residency — logs generated in EU regions stay in EU unless you configure cross-region export, right?
[14:20] Samir Patel: correct. we regionally store logs matching the request region; cross-region export must be explicitly enabled and will be called out in the contract for compliance review.
[14:40] Ella Park: on retention policies — can we set per-resource retention? e.g., longer retention for admin logs than for normal access logs?
[14:50] Samir Patel: yes, retention policies are configurable by event type. admin/privileged actions can have their own longer retention buckets and separate export/hold rules.
[15:10] Maya Thompson: can you run a sample POC where you export 24 hours of admin logs into our Splunk instance? we'll want to validate fields and alerts.
[15:20] Jordan Lee: absolutely, that's our suggested next step. samir will provide sample logs and the export config; then we'll set up a 24h POC export.
[15:35] Maya Thompson: timeline question — SOC2 audit is scheduled late July, so we need artifacts by mid-July. is that feasible?
[15:45] Jordan Lee: yes, we can prioritize the artifact collection. i'll get you the SOC2 Type II report and the audit log schema by Friday.
[16:00] Carlos Ruiz: minor nit — do you rotate the request_id format? we want immutable correlation ids that we can use across downstream processing.
[16:10] Samir Patel: request_id is a UUID v4 currently, stable per request. if you need a custom correlation pattern we can introduce an upstream mapping layer in Dedicated.
[16:30] Ella Park: about access reviews — will you provide quarterly access review exports so we can reconcile who had access to logs?
[16:40] Samir Patel: yes, we export RBAC reports and access review logs. those are available as a periodic report or on-demand CSV export.
[17:00] Maya Thompson: if we enable BYOK for KMS, how do key rotation events appear in the logs?
[17:10] Samir Patel: key rotation events are logged with old_key_id/new_key_id, rotation_time, actor, and the scope (account/region). we also capture failed rotation attempts and alerts.
[17:35] Jordan Lee: i want to call out a common ask — customers want to tie audit logs to product telemetry to debug production incidents. we support correlating product traces with audit events via the shared request_id.
[17:50] Carlos Ruiz: ok great. another compliance question — do you provide copies of logs for auditors?
[17:58] Samir Patel: yes, for audits we can provide time-bounded immutable exports, signed digests, and accompanied SOC2/ISO evidence. those exports can be delivered to your secure S3 or via an encrypted transfer.
[18:20] Maya Thompson: any red flags or gotchas we should be aware of?
[18:25] Samir Patel: main one is ensuring you don't enable expanded content capture broadly — make it scoped. also, if you need extremely long retention on hosted, cost and contractual terms need to be addressed. and ensure SSO assertion attributes map correctly so user identities line up in your SIEM.
[18:50] Jordan Lee: now i'll open it up for anything we missed.
[19:00] Maya Thompson: what about retention deletion proofs — can you show evidence that a deletion occurred (or that it was prevented by legal hold)?
[19:10] Samir Patel: yes we maintain deletion audit trails and when legal hold is active, deletes for that artifact are blocked and the attempted delete is logged as an event. we can provide an immutable audit of deletion attempts.
[19:35] Ella Park: do you support FIPS endpoints for syslog/tls? our auditors want FIPS-compliant crypto.
[19:45] Samir Patel: we support TLS 1.2/1.3 and can offer FIPS-certified endpoints for Dedicated/Private under enterprise agreements. i'll note that as a requirement in the follow-up.
[20:05] Carlos Ruiz: about scale — if we put a lot of automated jobs talking to Redwood, can we tag service accounts separately so we can filter logs?
[20:15] Samir Patel: yes, service accounts have their own actor type and can be filtered; we also support tagging and structured metadata so you can partition logs.
[20:35] Maya Thompson: ok that's helpful. last question: can we run a daily digest of admin role changes to an email distribution?
[20:45] Samir Patel: yes, daily digest or immediate notification; configurable by rule.
[20:55] Jordan Lee: great, time check — we're at about 21 minutes in, but sounds like we covered a lot. any remaining items?
[21:05] Maya Thompson: just one ask: please include sample redacted logs and the exact export schema in your follow-up.
[21:15] Samir Patel: will do.
[21:20] Jordan Lee: okay recap and next steps — Jordan will send SOC2 Type II report and the audit log schema by 2026-06-26, Samir will share sample S3 export and a Splunk ingestion guide by 2026-06-29, Haven will confirm retention/legal hold constraints by 2026-07-02, and we'll tentatively schedule the 24h POC export for the week of 2026-07-08.
[21:45] Maya Thompson: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[21:50] Jordan Lee: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links to the docs and sample logs.
[21:55] (call ends)

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts present (product names autocorrected in slides). References to shared artifacts: SOC2 report (link to be shared), audit_log_schema.json (sample), sample_s3_export_redacted.json (sample).
